opus-5.5.text:
I think simulation is really interesting, but I'd frame it a little differently from how people often talk about it. There's a tempting idea that a sufficiently powerful system could just imagine the world, run lots of internal rollouts, and learn everything it needs from that. And I think that's partly right, but the catch is that a simulation is only as good as the model that generates it, and the model only gets good by being grounded in real experience.

So the way I'd think about it is that self-generated simulation is a tool for making better use of the experience you already have. When people plan, they imagine counterfactuals: what would happen if I did this instead of that? That lets you squeeze much more learning out of a limited amount of real interaction. You can rehearse, consider alternatives, and refine your strategy without paying the cost of trying everything for real. For an AI system, especially one acting in the physical world where data is expensive, that's hugely valuable.

But I don't think simulation substitutes for interacting with the world. The really important thing is the loop: you act, you see what actually happens, you notice where your predictions were wrong, and you correct your model. The surprises are where the information is. If you only learn from your own imagination, you can get very confident about things that are simply false, because nothing in the loop forces you to confront reality.

And in some ways the most powerful version isn't a literal pixel-level simulator anyway. It's more like having good representations of the world that let you reason about the consequences of your actions at the right level of abstraction. Humans don't simulate every photon when they plan to make breakfast; they reason about objects, goals, and what's likely to happen. I think a really capable AI system will do something similar: use internal simulation and reasoning to amplify its experience, while staying anchored by continual real-world feedback. That combination, rather than either piece alone, is what I'd expect to lead to systems that understand the world.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation is only as good as a model grounded in real experience, and that learning only from imagination cannot force contact with reality. This communicates that self-generated experience alone does not add new information about the world.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss classical robotics simulation or explain that it transfers human knowledge into a robot.

r003.rationale: The response discusses simulation and reasoning as tools, but does not suggest that a highly capable model is probably the most powerful source of synthetic experience.

r004.rationale: The response does not address evaluating a powerful AI as a black box or say that simulation versus a model-free method is irrelevant to understanding its capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really interesting question, and it's one where I've gone back and forth a bit in my own thinking over the years. The way I'd frame it is that there are really two different things that people mean when they talk about simulation in the context of learning agents.

One is the sort of engineering notion of a simulator: you build a physics engine, you render some scenes, you train your robot in there and hope it transfers. That's useful, and a lot of the field has gotten mileage out of it, but it's fundamentally limited by the fidelity of what a human can write down. The simulator only knows about the things the engineer thought to put in it.

The other notion, which I think is the more interesting one for very powerful systems, is the idea of a learned model of the world, something the agent builds up from its own experience. And here the crucial thing is that the "simulation" isn't a separate artifact that gets handed to the agent. It's an internal capability. The agent has seen a lot of data about how the world responds to its actions, and it can use that to imagine, roughly, what would happen if it did something it hasn't actually tried yet.

Now, the reason I think this matters so much is that it changes what learning from experience even means. If you can only learn from things that actually happened to you, you're bottlenecked on how much you can physically interact with the world. A robot can only do so many trials in a day. But if you can take the experience you've had and extrapolate from it, essentially running counterfactuals in your head, then a small amount of real experience can go a very long way. That's a big part of what makes humans so sample-efficient. You don't have to touch the stove a hundred times.

There's a subtlety, though, that I think people sometimes gloss over. A learned model is always going to be wrong in some ways, and it's going to be most wrong precisely in the places where the agent has the least data, which are often exactly the places where you'd want to use it to plan. So you get this failure mode where the agent imagines a sequence of actions, the model says "great, this will work," and it only works because the model is being exploited in regions where it's unreliable. Any serious use of self-generated simulation has to be paired with some way of knowing what you don't know, some form of epistemic humility built into the system, so it can tell the difference between "I've simulated this and I'm confident" and "I've simulated this and I'm basically hallucinating."

The other thing I'd say is that I've become somewhat skeptical of the clean separation between the model and the policy. In the classical model-based RL picture you learn a dynamics model, you plan with it, you get a policy. But I think in really capable systems these things blur together. The representation that lets you predict what's going to happen is often the same representation that lets you decide what to do. And something like a large pretrained model is already, in some sense, a simulator, not of physics necessarily, but of what plausibly comes next. So the self-generated simulation might not look like a traditional simulator at all. It might just be the system's own forward reasoning about consequences.

So I guess the short version is: I think self-generated simulation is going to be central, but less as a distinct module and more as a property of what it means to understand the world well enough to act in it. The question that I think is still genuinely open is how you ground that imagination in real experience tightly enough that it stays honest.

r002.rationale: It describes engineer-built physics engines for robot training and their fidelity limits, but does not explain that this transfers human knowledge into the robot.

r003.rationale: It calls learned simulation central to capable systems, but does not identify a highly capable model as probably the most powerful source of synthetic experience.

r004.rationale: It says model and policy can blur together, but does not argue that the distinction is irrelevant when assessing a powerful AI as a black box.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between generating more experience and generating more information. If you have a model of the world and you run simulations inside that model, you’re not getting new information about the world. But you can still learn something that you didn’t know how to compute before. Playing out a game of chess doesn’t tell you anything new about the rules, but it can tell you a lot about which moves are good.

So I would expect self-generated simulations to be very useful for a powerful AI system. You can take what you’ve learned from experience and use a lot more computation to work out its implications—to practice, to plan, to evaluate different strategies.

The difficulty is that, unlike chess, we don’t have the exact rules of the real world. Your simulator is an approximation. And if you optimize very hard against that approximation, you can find strategies that exploit mistakes in the simulator. They look great in your imagined world and fail in the real one.

That suggests a process where simulation and interaction complement each other. You imagine possible outcomes, identify an experiment that would distinguish between them, go perform that experiment, and update your model. The simulation helps you get more value out of each interaction. But you still need that connection to reality to correct things you’ve gotten wrong.

r001.rationale: It says simulations in a world model do not provide new information about the world, though they can help derive implications from existing experience.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss classical robotics simulation or transferring human knowledge into a robot.

r003.rationale: It says simulations are useful for a powerful AI, but does not claim a highly capable model is the most powerful source of synthetic experience.

r004.rationale: It does not assess a powerful AI as a black box or say whether it uses simulation versus a model-free method is irrelevant.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is where the information in that simulation comes from. If you have a model of the world, you can use it to imagine the consequences of different actions. That can be enormously useful, because actually trying those actions might be expensive or dangerous. But imagining something doesn’t, by itself, give you new evidence about the world. If your model is wrong, you can become very good at exploiting a mistake in your own model.

One way to think about this is that there are two different bottlenecks. One is acquiring information, and the other is figuring out the implications of information you already have. Self-generated simulations can help tremendously with the second. You might already know enough to solve a problem, but finding the solution requires working through a huge number of possibilities.

And then there’s an interaction between the two: you can use imagined experience to decide what real experience would be most informative. You might discover that two plausible explanations predict different outcomes for a particular action, and then go take that action. So I would expect a powerful system to alternate between imagining, acting, and updating its understanding. The simulation makes its interactions with the world more productive, and those interactions keep the simulation grounded.
